opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. My view is that at OpenAI, intelligence and product aren't really two separate tracks. They feed each other in a loop.

The core belief, from the beginning, was that the most important thing is to push the frontier of intelligence. If the model gets fundamentally smarter, a lot of product problems simply go away. You don't need clever engineering tricks to patch a weak model. So the research mindset came first: scale things up, find the next paradigm, make the model better at reasoning.

But I think people sometimes misunderstand product as a distraction from research. In practice, product turned out to be a very important part of the research. ChatGPT is a good example. Before it launched, nobody really knew how people would use a chat model, or which capabilities mattered most. Once you put it in front of hundreds of millions of people, you get an enormous amount of signal: where it fails, what people care about, what "helpful" actually means. That feeds back into training, data, and evaluation. So product is a kind of grounding. It keeps intelligence from becoming a number on a benchmark.

There's also a practical side. Training frontier models is extremely expensive. Product brings revenue, which buys compute, which lets you train the next, better model. It's a flywheel. Without a successful product, it's very hard to sustain the pursuit of AGI at that scale.

That said, there is real tension. Every company has limited people and limited GPUs. If you spend too much on polishing the current product, you might miss the next paradigm shift. If you only do research, you might build something amazing that nobody uses, or that's unsafe once it meets the real world. My impression is that OpenAI's philosophy is roughly: intelligence is the main line, and product is how you test, fund, and deploy that intelligence responsibly. When it works well, the best product decision and the best research decision are actually the same decision.

One more thing, from my own background in reinforcement learning: as models become more agentic, the line blurs even more. An agent's capability is about how well it completes real tasks in real environments. The product environment is literally where the model learns and is evaluated. So I expect the boundary between "making the model smarter" and "making the product better" to become even thinner going forward.

r001.rationale: The response says smarter models can resolve product problems, but does not present improved intelligence as the source of new products.

r002.rationale: It discusses tradeoffs and product feedback, but does not say progress continues despite individual product failures.

r003.rationale: It does not say core researchers have little need to consider product issues; it instead describes product as important to research.

r004.rationale: It does not mention a post-training team serving as an intermediary between research capabilities and product delivery.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that at OpenAI, intelligence came first and product came second, and that ordering was never really in question. From the beginning the thing people were actually chasing was better models. The product was more like a byproduct of that pursuit.

Take ChatGPT. It wasn't planned as a grand product launch. The internal view was that the model was already quite strong, GPT-3.5 and then GPT-4 were in the pipeline, and there was this question of how to let more people actually touch the capability. The chat interface was almost a demo. Nobody expected it to blow up the way it did. So in that case the product was a very thin wrapper over intelligence, and the intelligence is what did the work.

But I'd say the relationship is more of a loop than a one-way street. Once you have a product with real users, you get two things back. One is data and feedback about where the model fails, which tells you what to prioritize in the next generation. The other is a sense of what people actually want from intelligence, which is often different from what researchers imagine in the lab. Things like instruction following, refusing gracefully, being consistent over long conversations. Those became research problems because the product surfaced them.

So my understanding is something like this. The core bet is that if you keep pushing the frontier of intelligence, products will follow, and the better the model the less product engineering you need to make it useful. That's why so much of the resources go into training rather than into polishing features. At the same time, the product is how you learn where the frontier actually matters, and it's how you fund the next model. Those two things feed each other, but if you ask which one the company would sacrifice, the answer was always clear. Nobody would slow the model down to ship a feature.

astra-6.text:
I see them as two closely connected efforts. One is to push the boundaries of intelligence: can the model reason better, solve harder problems, and handle more complex tasks? The other is to turn those capabilities into something people can actually use. A stronger model creates possibilities, but it doesn’t automatically create a good product. You still have to think about reliability, speed, cost, and how people interact with it.

And the relationship goes both ways. Once people use a product, you discover gaps that benchmarks may not capture. A model might perform very well on a test yet struggle to understand what a user wants over a longer interaction. Those experiences help clarify what needs to improve.

So I wouldn’t frame it as research versus products. Ideally, advances in intelligence make the products more useful, and product experience gives the research a clearer sense of which capabilities matter. The challenge is balancing immediate product needs with research whose value may take longer to emerge.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as two parts of the same feedback loop. Better intelligence expands what a product can do, while putting that intelligence into a product reveals what people actually need and where the model still falls short.

But they operate on different timelines. Research might produce a capability before we know how to make it useful, reliable, or easy to use. Product development turns that capability into something people can depend on. A stronger model doesn’t automatically mean a better product—you also need the right interface, responsiveness, and a clear understanding of the task.

So the challenge is to let real-world use inform research without allowing immediate product demands to define the entire research agenda. You need room to pursue longer-term advances, alongside the discipline of making today’s capabilities genuinely useful.
